## Supplementary Note 1: Sensitivity of the decomposition to duplicate and proxy traits

GPMap often holds several genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of the same
trait, together with traits that are defined by it or that track it closely.
Phenome-wide factor methods tolerate this redundancy. Our decomposition is more
sensitive to it, for two reasons that follow from its design: the pleiotropy
matrix holds only colocalising associations, and its variants are selected on
the target trait. This note describes the mechanism, the trait filters we apply
to counter it, and their effect in two traits.

### Why full-summary-statistic methods tolerate duplicates

GFA [1], GUIDE [2] and PathGPS [3] factorise a matrix in which every trait has
an estimated effect at every variant. A second, lower-powered GWAS of a trait
therefore has a row that is approximately a scaled copy of the first: its
z-scores are proportional to those of the original trait, plus sampling noise.
A linear factor model represents a scaled copy with the factor that already
represents the original trait, so the copy adds weight to that factor without
creating a new one. Consistent with this, GUIDE deliberately includes traits
correlated with its focal trait (r² > 0.5) in its trait-specific analyses [2],
and PathGPS removes no traits [3]. GFA removed near-identical traits in one
application, a panel of blood-cell traits measured in the same individuals,
because their highly correlated residuals made the fit numerically unstable;
it otherwise retains correlated traits [1].

### Why a colocalisation-based matrix does not

In our matrix a cell is observed only where the background trait colocalises
with the target trait at that locus, and an unobserved cell is fitted as an
observed zero with standard error 1 (Methods). Whether a trait colocalises at a
locus depends on its power, because it must carry an association signal there
strong enough to be fine-mapped. A lower-powered copy of a trait therefore
colocalises only at the loci where the original trait's effect is largest. Its
row is no longer a scaled copy of the original but a thresholded one, and the
threshold depends on the copy's power.

Supplementary Table 1 illustrates this with five target-trait loci and a second
GWAS of the same trait with one third of the power. With full summary
statistics, the second GWAS has expected z-scores of one third of the
original's, and the original trait's factor absorbs it. In the colocalisation
matrix, if for illustration a fine-mapped signal requires |z| > 5, the second
GWAS is observed at the first locus only. Its row is then not proportional to
the original: once the original trait's factor is fitted, the residual is
positive at the strongest locus and negative at the weaker ones, and empirical
Bayes matrix factorisation (EBMF) fits this contrast as a separate factor. That
factor marks loci with a large effect on the original trait, not a shared
mechanism. Copies of different power are thresholded at different points, and
each can contribute such a factor. Thresholding thus turns a linear copy, which
a linear factor model absorbs, into a non-linear one, which it does not.

**Supplementary Table 1.** Illustrative oriented z-scores for a target trait
and a second GWAS of the same trait with one third of the power.

| | Locus 1 | Locus 2 | Locus 3 | Locus 4 | Locus 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Target trait | 20 | 12 | 8 | 6 | 5 |
| Second GWAS, full summary statistics | 6.7 | 4.0 | 2.7 | 2.0 | 1.7 |
| Second GWAS, colocalising cells only | 6.7 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

This effect on the factorisation depends on fitting unobserved cells as zeros.
If unobserved cells were instead excluded from the likelihood, the observed
cells of a lower-powered copy would remain approximately proportional to the
original trait. We fit them as zeros because, in a matrix this sparse, which
cells are observed carries most of the information that separates programs;
a fit that skips unobserved cells collapses into one broad program (Methods).

### Proxies of the target trait

The problem is most severe for proxies of the target trait: other GWAS of the
target trait, and the diagnosis, medication use, family history and
complications of a target disease. Because every variant in the matrix is
associated with the target trait, these proxies are observed at its strongest
loci and, once each locus is oriented to the target-trait risk allele, are
positive wherever they are observed. Each therefore separates the target's loci
by the size of their effect on the target rather than by mechanism. For the
same reason the target-trait row is excluded from the variant–variant
similarity matrix used in program validation, and a proxy left in the matrix
reintroduces it. In a phenome-wide analysis, by contrast, variants are drawn
from associations with any trait, and a proxy row reinforces the factor of the
trait it stands in for.

In the type 2 diabetes (T2D) analysis benchmarked against the clusters of
Suzuki et al. [4], retaining 11 diabetes diagnosis, medication and
family-history traits produced an additional high-confidence program (20
variants, similarity z = 16) whose trait loadings rested entirely on those
traits and whose loci came from every Suzuki cluster. The number of
high-confidence programs fell from 11 to 8, and the number of programs
supported by Suzuki index variants (enrichment q ≤ 0.10) fell from 11 of 15 to
7 of 16. Mean background similarity did not change (0.029 in both fits),
because these traits colocalise only at the strongest loci, so a check of
background similarity alone would not have detected the problem.

### Redundancy among background traits

A second problem arises from redundancy among background traits. It takes two
forms: the same trait measured more than once (for example, a consortium GWAS
and the UK Biobank (UKB) field for the same trait, or the saddlepoint
approximation (SPA)- and Firth-corrected analyses of one UKB binary trait), and
traits whose effects share the target's sign at nearly every target locus (for
body mass index (BMI), body-size and body-composition measures). The matrix is
sparse: after duplicate and proxy removal, 2.2% of cells in the BMI matrix were
observed, and the median pair of variants shared one observed trait. A block of
well-powered, same-signed traits therefore makes up much of each variant's
observed profile and makes random pairs of variants appear similar. This raises
the background against which the program similarity test is calibrated, since
the test compares each program with random variant sets of the same size drawn
from the same matrix. The validation statistics also count each copy
separately: variant–variant similarity, connectedness and similarity z sum over
traits, and the effective number of traits counts each copy as a distinct
trait, so a program carried by several versions of one trait need not appear to
rest on a single trait. This second problem stems partly from the sparsity of
the colocalisation matrix and partly from the similarity-based validation, which
has no counterpart in the full-summary-statistic methods.

### Mitigation

We remove traits before building the matrix, using two lists that each pair a
trait with a parent trait.

- **Duplicates** are the same measurement imported into GPMap more than once,
  such as a repeated import of one GWAS, the left- and right-side versions of a
  body measure, or the SPA- and Firth-corrected versions of one UKB trait.
  GPMap maintains this list. The parent is retained and the copies are removed,
  whatever the target trait; if the target trait is itself listed as a copy,
  its parent is removed instead, so that one version of the measurement
  remains.
- **Proxies** are different traits that stand in for the same underlying
  trait, such as the diagnosis, medication use, family history and
  complications of a disease (family history is the basis of GWAS by proxy
  [5]), or body-size measures for BMI. Proxies are removed only when their
  parent is the target trait, and are currently curated by hand for each target
  from its colocalisation partners. A proxy of a background trait is retained,
  because it carries biology relevant to the target (body size in a T2D
  analysis), although it still counts more than once in the validation
  statistics.

Where background similarity remains high, correlated background traits can
additionally be removed with a concordance rule. For BMI, we removed
anthropometric and body-composition traits that were observed at 10 or more
BMI loci and whose oriented effect had the same sign at 80% or more of them.
The rule selected 40 traits, of which 14 had already been removed as GPMap
duplicates. Waist-to-hip ratio met the rule but was retained, because fat
distribution is what separates obesity sub-programs. We fitted BMI with and
without this rule; both fits removed 4 BMI proxies and 156 GPMap duplicates
(Supplementary Table 2).

**Supplementary Table 2.** BMI decomposition with and without removal of
correlated body-size traits (GPMap build of 12 October 2026).

| | Duplicates and proxies removed | Also 26 body-size traits removed |
|---|---|---|
| Background traits | 569 | 543 |
| Mean background similarity | 0.251 | 0.013 |
| Variant pairs with similarity ≥ 0.2 | 52% | 4.2% |
| High / medium-confidence programs | 4 / 2 | 7 / 6 |
| Low-confidence programs | 29 | 14 |
| Annotations with enrichment (trait categories / Reactome / KEGG) | 4 / 0 / 0 | 8 / 1 / 2 |

Removing 26 of 569 background traits (5%) reduced mean background similarity
about twentyfold and more than doubled the number of high- and
medium-confidence programs. In the first fit, half of all random variant pairs
already exceeded the connectedness threshold, so few programs could show that
their variants were more alike than chance.

Removing traits also removes observations. With the body-size traits removed,
1.0% of matrix cells were observed (against 2.2%), and the median pair of
variants shared no observed trait (against one), so many similarities rest on
few traits. A removed trait may also carry real biology. The aim is therefore
to remove the axis shared by every variant while keeping traits that differ
between variants, such as fat distribution.

We report background similarity for every fit. A high value indicates that
redundant background traits remain in the matrix. As the T2D example shows,
proxies of the target trait need not raise background similarity, which is why
they are removed by an explicit list rather than detected from the fit.

## Supplementary Note 2: Linkage disequilibrium

Phenome-wide factor methods work at the level of individual variants and must
handle linkage disequilibrium (LD) themselves: GFA clumps variants to r² < 0.01
within 1 Mb windows [1], and GUIDE does not explicitly account for LD [2]. Our
decomposition inherits its handling of LD from GPMap, which addresses LD before
any data enter the matrix [6]. GPMap partitions the genome into 1,357
approximately LD-independent regions [7], fine-maps each region with SuSiE [8]
against a European-ancestry UK Biobank LD reference panel, tests pairs of
fine-mapped signals for colocalisation using coloc on the SuSiE Bayes factors
[9], and groups colocalising signals across studies.

Two consequences follow. First, each column of the matrix is one fine-mapped
signal of the target trait (one colocalisation group), not a variant. Each
signal is therefore represented once, rather than by the many variants that tag
it, and no clumping or pruning step is needed. Second, a cell is observed only
when a background trait's fine-mapped signal colocalises with the target signal
(posterior probability of a shared causal variant ≥ 0.8). A background trait
therefore enters a column through evidence for a shared causal variant, not
merely through association at a nearby correlated variant.

Some LD-related limitations remain. Colocalisation cannot distinguish a single
causal variant shared by two traits from two distinct causal variants in strong
LD [10, 11], so an observed cell may reflect a distinct but highly correlated
variant; this limitation applies to any colocalisation-based analysis.
Fine-mapping assumes that distinct signals in a region can be separated [9],
and signals in the same or neighbouring regions may still be in partial LD. Our
enrichment analyses treat each signal as an independent observation, so their
p-values may be somewhat optimistic where nearby signals share annotations.

## Supplementary Note 3: Sample overlap

Many GWAS in GPMap share participants, most notably those drawn from UK
Biobank. Overlapping samples correlate the sampling errors of two studies'
estimates, approximately in proportion to the fraction of shared participants
multiplied by the phenotypic correlation of the two traits [10, 12]. This
produces correlation between the traits' summary statistics that is not
genetic.

Full-summary-statistic factor methods must model this, because most variants in
their matrices have little or no association with most traits, and the
cross-trait covariance at those variants is dominated by correlated sampling
error. GFA estimates this covariance from cross-trait LD score regression
intercepts and includes it in the model as fixed factors [1], and PathGPS
subtracts a covariance estimated from variants without association signals [3].
Our matrix contains no such cells. A cell is observed only where a background
trait has a fine-mapped association signal that colocalises with the target
signal, and unobserved cells are fixed at zero rather than estimated.
Correlated sampling error can shift the value of an observed cell, but it does
not supply the fine-mapped, colocalising association that a cell requires.

The remaining question is whether overlap affects the colocalisation calls
themselves. Colocalisation methods compute the joint likelihood of two studies
as the product of their individual likelihoods, which assumes independent
samples [11, 12]. Simulations suggest that this assumption matters little in
practice. In HyPrColoc simulations of ten quantitative traits measured in the
same individuals, ignoring the overlap identified the cluster of colocalised
traits in 97.5% of simulations (residual correlation 0.5), compared with 95.5%
for traits measured in independent samples, with no increase in false
positives; results were similar for residual correlations of −0.1 and 0.8, and
adjusting the likelihood alone for overlap performed worse [12]. For two
quantitative traits measured in the same individuals, residual correlations up
to 0.8 likewise had a negligible effect on coloc posterior probabilities [13].
These simulations used quantitative traits only. They did not test case–control
traits, colocalisation on SuSiE output, or distinct causal variants in LD under
overlap, and the HyPrColoc authors describe their investigation as brief and
limited [12]. We did not model sample overlap explicitly.

GPMap's rare-variant results would be more exposed to overlap. They come from
exome-sequencing analyses of UK Biobank participants (Genebass, Backman et al.
and the AstraZeneca Genomics Initiative), so different traits' results share
most of their participants. Because the variants are absent from the LD
reference panel, these results are not fine-mapped or colocalised, and GPMap
instead groups traits that share a significant variant [6]. They would
therefore lack both protections described above. The decomposition uses only
common-variant colocalisation results, not rare-variant results.
